title: The Psalms, looking back
tomorrow: why would God ever tell a choir to stop singing?

lines: A PLAYLIST FOR THE BAD WEEKS.
WHAT DOES A HUNTED MAN SING?
cards: Some people keep a playlist for the bad weeks, songs that say it better than they can. One of the oldest starts in a cave.
David is on the run from King Saul, who is hunting him with his soldiers, and the rock walls are close and dark. A psalm's heading puts a song right there: when he fled from Saul in the cave.
Hunted, cornered, no way out but further in. And in the dark, he opens his mouth to sing. So what does a hunted man sing?

teach.b: He starts with the truth. “Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast.”
No pretending the cave is a palace.

teach.h: MY HEART IS FIXED: I WILL SING.
teach.b: A few lines later, the song turns: “My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise.” The fear isn't edited out. It's prayed through, to the other side.
Looking back, that's the pattern of the whole book.

teach.h: HOW LONG, THEN I WILL SING.
teach.b: Psalm thirteen opens, “How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?” and by its last line says, “I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me.”
Psalm thirty: “weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.” Psalm forty-two talks to itself: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul?”
Anger, fear, guilt, wonder: all of it said to God rather than hidden from God. Here's one to tell a friend tonight.
In Matthew's Gospel, when Jesus cries out on the cross, my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, he is praying the opening line of Psalm twenty-two.
These are Israel's songs, still prayed in synagogues, and Christians pray them too, some in a daily round, some one psalm on a hard night.

how: Christians pray and sing the Psalms in worship, and some pray them through in a daily round of morning and evening prayer; Jews pray the Psalms in the synagogue and at home.

o: cheerful hymns written only for church holidays
Israel's songs and prayers, with every feeling given words
a book of rules for running the Temple

games.q: songs for every feeling — tap the pairs.
p: how long, then I will sing
the line Jesus cries from the cross

s: the Psalms are mostly calm, cheerful hymns
they hold how long, why art thou cast down, and a song from a cave.
Jesus's cry from the cross is the opening line of a psalm
Psalm 22: my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me.
in Psalm 57, David waits until he's safe before he sings
the heading puts the song in the cave, while Saul is still hunting him.

games.q: your friend's dog died this morning. she says she can't pray, because it would only be complaining. what do the Psalms offer her?
o: wait a few days, until she can pray thankfully again.
bring the complaint itself to God: how long, why. the Psalms do.
pray a cheerful psalm instead, to lift her mood first.
games.why: Psalm 13 starts with how long and is still a prayer, and David's song starts with be merciful unto me. the feeling goes to God, not around God.

practice: Say one line out loud, quietly, the one closest to how today actually is: how long, or why art thou cast down, or joy cometh in the morning, or I will sing.

Say it twice, slowly, and let the sit hold the rest; if you pray, pray it as your own. If a feeling is too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: The Psalms. Israel's book of songs and prayers, where every feeling, from how long to I will sing, is given words.

orig.note: Hebrew: Tehillim, the name of the book of Psalms.

carryVoice: Your line: pray what you feel, the way a hunted man sang in a cave. Fourteen days into the summit.
